utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We are moving to the next stage of these proceedings, after we have heard the case presentation by the Prosecution and the presentation of its case by the Defence. The Chamber, as it was announced yesterday, the Chamber after having heard the witnesses called by the parties, decided to call a number of Chamber witnesses pursuant to Rule 98 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Among these witnesses is Mr. Amir Delic. The Chamber contacted him on the 20th of June, 2006. The Chamber then informed the parties about its intention to call Mr. Delic, and Mr. Delic appears today without any protective measures. Mr. Josse, the Chamber was informed that you would like to address Chamber in private session. Should that be when the witness has entered the courtroom or before he enters the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Before, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness, Mr. Delic, into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Delic, I assume. Mr. Delic, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require to you make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The usher will now hand out the text of this solemn declaration in your own language, and may I invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Delic. Mr. Delic, you are called as a witness by this Chamber. I would first like you to tell the Court your full name.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Amir Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And your date of birth, Mr. Delic, is?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: The 18th of September, 1958.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move for a moment into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, could you please give D116A -- I wanted to say to Mr. Usher to have it put on the ELMO. Mr. Delic -- Could we zoom out a little bit so we have the whole of the photograph on -- yes. Thank you. Mr. Delic, this photograph is in evidence before this Chamber. I would like to ask you a few questions about this photograph. First of all, do you recognise the persons on this photograph, and would you please start from the left and tell us who is on the photograph and what positions they held at the time?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: The first person on the left is myself. Next to me is Mr. Zunic. I think he was a representative of the army of the Autonomous District of Krajina, from Dvor. I knew him personally before. He was the technical manager of the Dvor hauliers. I am an engineer in traffic, and I worked at the Bosanski Novi and we were business associates. Next to him is the chief -- the municipality mayor, Radomir Pasic. Next to him is the representative of the international community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I -- you were pointing already at the fourth person but you say the one in the dark suit is Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then the next one with the -- without a jacket is you said --

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Without the jacket, holding a pencil and a pad in his hand, is the gentleman representing the UNHCR, and I believe he was called, although I can't be certain, Jansen, Nilsen or something such-like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the next one with the camouflage coloured --

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Wearing a camouflage uniform is Mr. Nikola, also from Dvor Na Uni. To my knowledge, he was the police commander there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then the last person?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: The last person is Mr. Emir Puric, my friend and my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Delic, do you remember the occasion at which this photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. The photograph was taken during the negotiations process at the bridge between Bosanski Novi and the Matijevic neighbourhood. This is a bridge on the Una and the village lies in the direction of Dvor Na Uni.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was this the first negotiations you held at that time or was it a follow-up of any earlier negotiations?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: This was a follow-up of earlier negotiations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many earlier negotiations had been -- had taken place?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you the precise number, but I can chronologically set out the events in the period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll come to that later. What was the subject of the negotiations? What were you negotiating about?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: The subject of negotiations was the departure of Croats and -- Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims in a convoy from Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Why did this meeting take place on a bridge?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Well, I would have to give you a more general picture, and I should perhaps start with the start of the negotiations, how they came about, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please try to listen to me carefully as well. I'll give you an opportunity now to start to tell us on from the start what caused the need for negotiations, but I might have some questions in between, so I would then stop you and perhaps ask for further details. But please start with telling us what caused you, or if you are not involved as a person but as a representative of any group or organisation, what caused you to enter into negotiations at all.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: In 1991 and 1992, the situation in Bosanski Novi was disastrous; one could put it that way. All the events taking place in the Republic of Croatia had a direct impact on the situation in Bosanski Novi. That period I won't be touching upon again. I just wanted to introduce the situation. On the 11th of May, 1992, in the early morning hours, shooting started all around the town. Shots were fired from various weapons. One could hear individual shots --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I stop you there already? On the 11th of May, where were you living at the time? In town, in Bosanski Novi town? Or in a --

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I wasn't married at the time. I lived on my own in a two-bedroom apartment in a building called Sivi Dom. My parents had their own home in the immediate vicinity of that building within some 200 or 300 metres. On the 10th of May, in the afternoon hours, a strange atmosphere reigned in the town. My brother, my sister-in-law and their children, myself, neighbour Admir Ceric and lady neighbour Amra Dautcehajic, went to my apartment. We left the family house and went into my apartment in the building where we believed we would be safer. At the time there were uniformed persons going from door to door, taking away the male population. That was why we thought that as a group we would be more protected and safer. That is why we all went to my apartment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you talking about the town only and are you talking about what you observed personally?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us, if you say taking away the male population, what exactly did you see in that respect?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Specifically, there was a red van, Renault Traffic making rounds in the town, and it was common knowledge that there were uniformed persons who would round up people and then take them to -- for interrogation to either the police station or the fire department building. I myself didn't see any of the persons who had been taken over there, but I did see the van going around the town from my apartment window.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you went to your apartment. What did you further observe?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: We were in the apartment. As I said, in the morning, shooting was heard. There was live coverage of the events on Radio Bosanski Novi. Muslims were called upon over the radio to surrender weapons. And they were told that no harm would come to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that call to hand in weapons, was that specifically addressed to Muslims or to other nationalities as well?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: It was addressed to Muslims because the numbers of Croats and other non-Serbs living in Bosanski Novi were negligible. I apologise. I would like to say the following, that probably being excited here, I just want to touch upon the following. The -- it wasn't on that date that my brother and my sister-in-law and their children went to my apartment; rather, that happened on the 31st of May or between the 31st of May and the 1st of June. On that previous date it was just myself. I was by myself in my apartment. The rest of my statement, however, is accurate. In the morning, and it was a Monday, we were not able to go to work. In -- during the morning, I went back to my parents' house, to see them. Since my home is directly opposite from a school centre, people from the neighbourhood of Prekosanje and Urije, under the escort of a blue combat vehicle and armed soldiers, whilst carrying visible white flags, arrived to the school centre. Most of the people were put up at the school centre. There were women, children, men, elderly people. In fact, that was the entire population of these two neighbourhoods. We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I stop you? We have received a map in evidence. You were talking about Urije. Is that Urije which is on a map a little bit to the east of town?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Upstream, the Sana river. Prekosanje is across the Sana river.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Urije is at a distance of some three kilometres from the centre of town, as I see on a map? If would you like to have a look at it you can take a look, but is that approximately the distance?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, roughly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Us neighbours who had their homes across from the school centre took up food and other items to take them to the people, to help them, and I mean those who were put up at the school centre. Some of the people who had relatives or friends in the Vidorija neighbourhood where the school centre is were able to find accommodation in private homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you did you recognise any of the people that were brought to that school? Did you know any of them?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. For instance, Professor Jasmin Custic and his family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now the population of the areas you talked about, including Urije, do you know whether people living there were of what nationality or ethnicity mainly?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Mostly Muslims, Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you see any Serb among the people who were taken to the school? So I'm not talking about who took them to the school but people that were taken to the school centre.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: No. At Prekosanje the people who refused to abandon their homes were killed at the doorstep of their homes. I didn't witness that myself, but this is what I was told by the people who came to the school centre. Among others, the father of my friend Elvira Mujkic was killed at the threshold of his house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you told us that people were taken to the school centre but some who had, who would know people living around in the neighbourhood, that they were able to find accommodation in private homes. Does that mean that they were not bound to stay in the school centre but they were free to go to friends' and stay with them? Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. The town was divided by check-points. This part of town, that's to say from Vidorija mosque, next to the hotel had its check-point. That was where people entered this part of town. And from that point, all the way to the other end of the town, at Mlakve, they could be accommodated wherever they pleased. In other words, if they had friends or relatives there, they could stay at their places. Those who had nowhere to go stayed at the school centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue to tell us what further happened on that day and perhaps the following days.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: We were trying to help those people to bring them food, freshen them up, and that was where they spent the night. Generally the situation in the town was settling down. Some of the people even started returning to their homes, if their homes hadn't been burned down. Of course, it took a lot of courage to go back, but people were highly motivated because they had left their homes with only a few personal belongings. This sort of atmosphere existed in the town until the 31st of May, which was a Sunday. I was mentioning the afternoon hours, and my brother and my sister-in-law and Cehajic, my neighbour, that was when all of us went to my apartment. At about 10.00 or 11.00 at night, at any rate it was night-time, shooting resumed. Different cars with the rotating light and sirens circled the town, and torching started. From my living-room window and balcony, one could see the town mosque aflame as well as the Vidorija mosque. That was also burning. At the other end of the apartment, there was the kitchen from where I could see two houses on fire across from the street next to the tunnel. That was the house of Heder Sead and the house of Sead Ceric. Sead Heder with his wife, children and his elderly mother fled to the entranceway of our building, of our apartment block, and I took them into my apartment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you the persons you are talking about, starting on the 31st of May, could you tell us what was their nationality or ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Muslims, Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the owners of the houses that you saw to be torched, could you tell us what their nationality and ethnicity was?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: They were Muslims, Sead Heder, and Sead, Seric, also known as Sejo [phoen], or Ribar [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to who put those houses in flames?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: No, no. I said that military vehicles were going around the town, and those were Pinzgauers with rotating lights, and sirens could be heard wailing, but I can't say who they were. We were only able to see two persons running toward the house and then we could see these houses suddenly on flame, especially Heder's house was -- caught fire quite quickly because it was an old house, a wooden house. In the immediate vicinity of my house, there is the handicraft or artisan's centre with some ten small workshops. We saw people entering them and then coming out carrying things. They were probably throwing grenades at them because we could hear explosions afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What then happened?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: That lasted all night. I have to say that the telephone lines were still working, and one could communicate with friends and family and we talked to them to find out whether they were still at their homes and what was going on with them. The next morning, groups of armed soldiers carrying automatic rifles were deployed in my street. We called it under the Jablanica. It was a former thoroughfare, former Boris Kidric Street; it's a dead end. So groups of two, three, four soldiers remained deployed in the street at a distance of 50 or so metres from one another, whereas two soldiers entered my entranceway. They went from one flat to another, entered and took out all the men. They were carrying a list. There was a list of names, including my name, and a number of a pistol against it. The fact is that as the technical director of the forwarding company, Kozara Prevoz in Bosanski Novi, according to regulations, was supposed to have a pistol, and it was properly licensed by the MUP, the authorities. I don't know which year it was issued, 1989 or 1990. Anyway, they found my name and they asked me to hand over the gun. I did hand it over. I asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you one question in this respect? You earlier told us that Muslims were called upon to hand over arms through the radio. Was that registered weapons included or unregistered -- and -- yes?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: No. That was on the 11th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: On the radio, when we had this practically live broadcast of the war, wherein the Muslims were attacking the town, they read out around ten names on the radio who allegedly had rifles. They even read out the numbers of those rifles. In that period, I'm not sure whether it was the 11th of May or some other date, but it was related to the -- it was around the 11th of May, the president of the social accountancy service of Bosanski Novi, Mr. Muhamedagic addressed people over the radio and said that the people who were read out as having the weapons actually had them, they should hand them over. I don't know what came of all that, whether the weapons were surrendered, whether they had been purchased in the first place. I don't know what happened to those ten persons. Some of them were allegedly arrested, but I really don't know what became of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would not mind, I would like to take you back again to that 11th of May. You started your last answer by saying, on the radio, when we had this practically live broadcast of the war wherein the Muslims were attacking the town, you have not told us before about an attack by Muslims on the town. Could you please explain when that took place, how it happened, from where?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: When that gun-fire started in early morning hours on the 11th of May, it was said on the radio that Muslims were attacking the place, that Green Berets are sowing death, that snipers were shooting all over town, and what remains particularly etched in my memory is that the Sudic [phoen] house which was at the entrance to the Urije neighbourhood had people in it shooting at Repovac from sniper rifles. An appeal was made to them to surrender, but according to my knowledge, although I was not an eyewitness, none of it happened. There was no such gun-fire from Muslim guns or no such organisation. At that time, people from Prekosanje, as I said earlier, were escorted to the school centre by combat vehicles through the high street. From Urije and Prekosanje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you very specifically: Is there any other source that would ever, whether you consider it a reliable source or not a reliable source, but was there any other source that confirmed what you heard on the radio, that is that Muslims were using firearms attacking the town or at least I take it attacking non-Muslims from Muslim positions?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: No. There were no Muslim positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you in that respect whether you ever heard or received any information about an attack on a military police patrol which was passing through a Muslim settlement in Bosanski Novi municipality on the 10th or around the 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was also announced on the radio that a patrol had been attacked, a patrol of the military police or some other police force. It was allegedly attacked in Blagaj which was seven or eight kilometres away from Bosanski Novi in the direction of Prijedor. And practically that is what started everything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I should invite you now to continue what you were telling us about what happened after the 31st of May, when soldiers were taking positions at least at the distance of 50 metres, going from -- to the flats. Yes.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: They were not taking up positions. They were standing in the middle of the road, in groups of two, three, four, soldiers. Whereas two soldiers entered my building. They were armed with automatic rifles and they went from one flat to another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know what forces they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: They wore military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have any idea about their nationality, ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't ask them for IDs and I cannot know but I suppose they were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Because at that time, when call-ups for mobilisation arrived in the post, Muslims did not respond to call-ups. I did not receive one myself because my wartime assignment was in my company, but of course I didn't get any. As for the apartment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps could you identify them on the basis of their uniforms as members of -- well, whatever armed force, police forces, TO forces, regular army?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Well, they wore the uniforms of the Yugoslav People's Army, the weapons, trousers, shirts, belts, everything that belongs to a uniform. I cannot tell you who wore which emblem, but I know that most of them had the emblem with the four letters S, but I cannot say with any certainty whether the two particular soldiers who came into my building had that emblem or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the 4 Ss is a Serb symbol? Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So please continue now where the two soldiers came to your apartment.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: So they found my name on the list. I handed over to them my pistol. But my brother's name was also on the list, because my brother was the commercial director of Stana service company and he also had a pistol licensed, et cetera. Since that pistol was in the house, because my brother occupied the upper floor of the house, we were taken to that house at gunpoint so that my brother can surrender his pistol. We asked the soldiers to give us receipts confirming that we had surrendered the pistols, because we were afraid that somebody else might come and ask for the same pistols again and we would not be able to prove that we had already surrendered them. The soldiers told us that there is no reason to fear that, that nobody else would come to ask for the same thing, after which we were taken back outside our building, and we were taken further up the street, to the square near the huntsman's hall, the huntsman's lodge, and there was a sort of podium put up there for performances and holidays and such. We were made to kneel and face the wall. We were forced to sing songs such as, "Comrade Tito," "Oj Kozara mountain" and I don't know what else. The soldiers fired around us, cursed and generally abused us, seeming to enjoy it. Then a bus belonging to my company arrived driven by Mr. Gajic, Mirko Gajic, a driver of the company, and they told us to get on the bus. When I entered the bus, it was already half full, so the driver made the man from the front seat get up so that I could sit down. I didn't want him to do that, and I sat down somewhere in the middle row. We were taken to the Sloboda stadium in Mlakve. That was around 10.00 or 11.00 when we arrived at the stadium.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you between, Mr. Gajic, what was his nationality or ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: A Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed. You said you were taken to the Mlakve stadium.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Of course, the stadium was encircled by soldiers and guards, and they let us in on to the grass field. There were already some people there. I don't know how many, but there were a lot of them. And all that day, buses kept bringing people to the stadium. And in the following days, the red van that kept driving around the town also brought some individuals, and there were also some people who walked to the stadium themselves. They came out of fear that they would be found at home and simply disappear. Homes were being searched, and once they were searched then the men from those homes were rounded up, had to hoist a white sheet outside the window which was a sign that the house was clear, quote unquote. At my home, the wife, children and mother of this man Sead, Heder whose house had been burned down were left behind. As for us, we remained at the stadium until Friday afternoon. I think it was the 5th or the 6th -- sorry, the 5th of June, when we were released and set free from the stadium to go home. On our first day at the stadium, we were given some tea and some liver paste but there was not enough for everybody so we had to share as best we could. And later on, since they obviously had not enough food for all of us, they allowed the families from the surrounding houses in that neighbourhood, Vidorija, to bring food to the stadium. So wives and mothers from the surrounding houses would put up the food on a table, the soldiers would inspect it, and then give it to us. We slept on the grass, whereas some people slept on the bleachers or in changing rooms, on pallets, anything they could get their hands on. One of the soldiers used a bullhorn to call out the names of Muslims, some particular Muslims, who were supposed to come out of the crowd, and one of them was Dzemo Sefer, the director of Privredna Banka in Prijedor, who was also a neighbour of mine. He was taken away somewhere, and I later learned that he had been taken to the police station. Some other people were called out and taken away, either to the hotel or to the fire department building for interrogation, and everything else that was implied. And one day - I think it was a Wednesday, but I'm not sure, it could have been Thursday as well - some buses arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Delic, could you tell us that you said -- first of all, one question. When, as you said, these men were -- people were rounded up, taken to the stadium where you stayed until, as you said, until Friday afternoon, does that mean that during the days you had then stayed at the stadium, you were not free to leave the stadium but that you were forced to stay within it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Of course. All around the stadium there were armed guards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you were allowed to leave the stadium on that Friday afternoon. Was everyone allowed to leave the stadium, as far as you're aware of, or was it you and others but not everyone?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned Dzemo Sefer and some other people who were called out before we were released and were taken away somewhere. And after that, it was said that the rest can go home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then you told us that you learned later that they were taken to either the hotel or the fire department building for interrogation. How did you learn about that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Since that part of town called Vidorija where my house is is small, we all know each other, because we all grew up together, because we were neighbours, and I know that when we left the stadium, a group of women was walking towards the municipality building to see what would become of us. One of them was Edina, the wife of Dzemo Sefer, Doda Molak, a maths teacher, and Rada Imsirevic, wife of Edo Imsirevic. However, nobody at the municipality wanted to receive them or give them an answer, and I found out, when I was released from the stadium, since we were not allowed to move out of our neighbourhood, we spent our time talking to each other and telling each other what we knew, sharing information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I take you back then to the moments where you said that buses arrived that could have been on the Thursday, some buses arrived. Where were you when those buses arrived? You returned to your own place before that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: No. I was at the stadium. By that time, nobody had gone back home. They told us when the buses arrived that we should all gather in the middle of the stadium and sit down. One of the commanders addressed us through a bullhorn, I know he was some sort of officer because he had some rank insignia but I couldn't recognise it, and he said that everybody who wanted to volunteer to join the Serb army should come out to sign up and go to the front line. And that started chaos among us. People asked a group of us who were sort of more educated or better known in the community what was the right thing to do, because we were all taken aback and astonished, and people took the following course of action. If there were two brothers together or a father and son together at the stadium, then one of them would sign up as a Serb volunteer and the other would stay at the stadium because the reasoning was that if they were not both on the same side, one would survive and be able to provide a living to their family. Some people fainted. I think three busloads of men, all in all, signed up. Of course, the army made records, lists, et cetera. According to the stories I heard later, those men were taken to Banja Luka to the Kozara barracks. However, they were brought back because Muslims or Turks, as they called them at the time, were not needed or wanted in the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you will continue, next Friday were you allowed to go home. Please keep in mind that one of the reasons why we called you as a witness is to hear more about the negotiations. We of course allow you to tell us what happened and what led to these negotiations. This Chamber also heard already some evidence on some of these events, so if you would please move forward and keep in the back of your mind that it's all an introduction why these negotiations were held. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: If I could just make a few more comments on the story and then I will move on. When we were at the stadium my uncle, Hasan Delic, was with me, and I mean at the camp on the stadium. We agreed that none of us should sleep at our homes upon returning there because Serbs might come around at night to round us up. I was sleeping in a shed. My uncle was sleeping at a place near the marketplace. That was on Friday evening. On Saturday, at around 10.00 in the morning, he returned home. Soon afterwards, he was taken out by some people and disappeared, went missing. Several days later, we were called to identify a body, and it was his body. He had been killed. His body had been abandoned near the Lignosper factory compound. I buried him in the town cemetery. There were nine bullets in all in the body, one of them at the back of his head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you who called you to identify the body of your uncle?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: My uncle -- my aunt, Marica, was called to identify him because she had reported him missing. She went to the police station, to the fire department building, to the hotel building, but nobody was able to tell her where he was. Finally, they called her over the phone to come to the mortuary to identify his body. I went over there with my other uncle who is now dead. We identified his body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has it ever been established or investigated who was responsible for the killing of your uncle?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I wish to make one more point concerning the stadium. While we were at the stadium, we were able to see people in white uniforms with binoculars, watching us. They were watching in the direction of the stadium and, of course, you have to keep in mind that the border between Croatia and Bosnia is near. When we went out of there on Friday afternoon, I met with my neighbour, Azemir Ceric, who had also been held at the stadium. Previously he was a police commander. I also met up with Mr. Emin Puric, another neighbour of mine. We were discussing what we should do next to save our skins. Since we had a common friend, Dragomir Drazic, a lawyer who used to work for the municipality, Emin Puric rang him, I believe it was a Sunday, and asked him to see us. He agreed to meet with us on Monday. I have to say that in the days and months leading up to that point, people who had had money and valuables were paying to be allowed to leave Bosnia through the Glina area for the purposes of medical treatment, quote unquote. That was the way for them to leave the area together with their families. I believe the sum required was 3.000 German marks per head, per capita, allegedly for medical treatment. We knew that there was an office of an international organisation, I will it was the EU monitors, UNPROFOR and so on, at Dvor Na Uni. Over the weekend, three of us decided to ask Drazic to help us leave Bosanski Novi somehow because the situation and matters in Bosanski Novi came to a head. He received us, and we told him that we wanted to leave the area and to save our skins. We said that we intended to go to Dvor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. A few questions in between. You were talking about people in white uniforms observing you. Were they on BiH territory or were they on the other side of the river? From where did they observe you when you were in the stadium?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: They were in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you said payments were made up to 3.000 German marks per head for -- allegedly for medical treatment. Payments were made to whom?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: You see, people had different connections or they tried to get hold of influential people, both in Bosanski Novi and at Dvor. The important thing was to cross the check-point on the bridge, and then once you reached Dvor, the people there would take you to Karlovac, where one would enter the Croatian territory. I don't know the specifics of it but I know of people who had left the area in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you understood that to be paying for buying your way out of the area? Is that a correct understanding of what you said? But do you have any further --

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any further details as to whom the payments were made?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: No. Of course, influential people who were able to materialise this and who made promises to do that were paid. Certainly these were no ordinary privates or soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Delic, finally, Mr. Drazic was of what nationality or ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Serb ethnicity. I have to say that Mr. Drazic was a work associate of Mr. Puric and a friend of Azemir Ceric because Drazic's daughter was a basketball player, and whilst they worked at Sana, Sana sponsored the basketball club. Mr. Ceric himself played basketball. I had business connections with Mr. Drazic while he worked at Lignosper. I can say that we were quite close acquaintances and that was the reason why we approached him to assist us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, I'm looking at the clock. It's time for a break. Mr. Delic, perhaps during the break, you can -- I take it that we are now approximately at the point where you start speaking with or negotiating with whomever. So I would like very much to spend, well, let's say the next half an hour after the break on to whom you did speak, what was the subject and perhaps first take us through the main lines and if we need to know any further details, we'll certainly ask you about it. We will have a break until 11.30 but then really 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, before the break, we came to the point where you and I think you said Mr. Puric wanted to discuss with Mr. Drazic, who was a Serb acquaintance of you, what to do. Could you please continue?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He received us on Monday in the municipal building. Azemir Ceric, Emin Puric and I were at the meeting. We asked him to help us in fleeing the area. We also told him that we intended to go to Dvor to apply to the representatives of the international community there to help us. He said that he was unable to give us an answer there and then but that he would look into what the situation was in the municipality and that he would get in touch with us. The following day he got in touch with Mr. Puric and said that the authorities were not opposed to us leaving and approaching the international community. He thought that we would be able to leave the town without any difficulties. The following day, in my father's -- in my brother's car, Emin Puric, a Serb friend of ours -- or, rather, there was Emin Puric and I and a Serb friend of ours whose name I do not wish to mention here, I don't want to cause any problems to him, drove us across the bridge. We went past the check-point there and stopped at the hotel in Dvor Na Uni. We were received by a lady there, I believe her name was Mirjana, and I think she was an interpreter there. We waited there for quite some time, three to four hours, before some people who had their head office in Topusko arrived, and they were the people we were supposed to talk to. Two of them came and I think that they were European monitors. We told them the whole story and related all the previous events, just as I have done to you now. We signed statements, I believe they were, or minutes or something of the sort, and I believe they also took our photographs. They told us to go back home and wait. We went back home, and several days passed without us receiving any news. I have to tell you that on our return, and it was in the evening, we decided that we should act as representatives of our neighbourhood, representing our neighbours and relatives. Neither I nor Mr. Puric were political activists. We were not members of any political party or any political organisation for that matter. Since our houses were next to each other, we decided nevertheless that we should represent them. On that day, we had set out early in the morning and returned back home late in the afternoon. People were already concerned about us and worried for us. At any rate, we became representatives of -- or leaders, so to speak, of the people there, of the citizens. Several days passed without us having received any news, which was why we asked this Serb friend of ours to take us back to Dvor again. We went to the headquarters of the Danish Battalion in the construction company complex called Rad. We were stopped at the gate where we were told that they were aware of our case, that it was being looked into and that we should go back home. We returned again. I can't give you the precise dates of all these trips because it's been a while. One day, a UNHCR vehicle showed up somewhere between Emin's house and my own. There were three people in the car. One of them was the person depicted on the photo called either Jansen or Nilsen, an interpreter and a journalist. We were sitting in Emin Puric's house. They brought Drazic along. We sat down and talked. He kept telling us that they didn't have the mandate to help us move out, that it amounted to ethnic cleansing, that they were merely able to provide us with humanitarian aid and food to alleviate the crisis, but that we should be patient. We would not agree to that. We insisted on us leaving and -- in view of these preceding events and the general situation. Several days later, we went to the Bosanski Novi municipal building to see the municipal mayor, Radomir Pasic. These were supposed to be negotiations, talks. He told us that they were not opposed to the idea of us moving out because we thought that we could not stay there any longer, especially in view much the fact that he could not guarantee safety for us. He said that in agreement with the municipal Crisis Staff, a decision would be taken regulating who would be able to leave and how. He said that most of the people would be allowed to leave but not the extremists. I don't know what he meant by that. However, at a later stage, rules were placed next to the entrance to the municipal building regulating who was able to leave. I was not allowed to go into these institutions where one could obtain documents allowing the person to leave and my brother had to go instead. We had to, for instance, obtain a document from the land registry office of Bosanski Novi certifying that we did not own any properties, or if we owned any properties, we were required to draft a contract where we would leave the property to the Serbs or to the Serb state or simply renouncing the property. Another document that had to be made was a list of all the members of the household. The third document that had to be produced was the certificate certifying that we had no previous convictions. Another document had to certify that we had covered all the utility bills, that there were no outstanding bills to all the utility companies in the town, including electricity, gas, water and so on and so forth. Another document had to be produced which stated that the municipal Secretariat for National Defence allowed that particular military conscript to leave the area of the municipality of Bosanski Novi. Another document had to be obtained from the municipal police allowing the applicant to leave. I forget whether there were any other documents, but all the documents had to state that what we were doing was on a voluntary basis and without duress. There were stories around the town that once a person went to the police station to obtain one such document, he or she would be arrested. This was a relatively small town, and people knew what was going on. I didn't dare to go obtain documents for me. My brother did that instead, and I stayed at home in hiding. As far as the negotiations are concerned for the free departure of the convoy, at one such meeting it was said that the SAO Krajina, or, rather, the Dvor Na Uni authorities would allow us free passage through SAO Krajina, and the two gentlemen depicted on the photograph, Mr. Zunic and Mr. Nikola, orally confirmed that. However, the problem lay in the fact that the Republic of Croatia refused to receive any further convoys with refugees. We insisted that we should be allowed to leave. Mr. Dragomir Pasic also insisted with the UNHCR representatives that we be allowed to leave. They told us, in turn, that we would not be allowed entry into the Republic of Croatia, or, rather, that we would not be allowed to get past the bridge, as we used to say. But since the situation was dreadful, we were resolute in our wish to leave. This took place on the 16th of July. Meanwhile, representatives of the international community showed up at the bridge and invited us for negotiations. In fact, they tried once again to dissuade us from leaving, pointing to all the difficulties and risks that it involved. I have a tape with me here where part of the negotiations was recorded, not the entire negotiations but one part of it anyway. One can see there what the subject of discussion was. We fixed the date of departure of the convoy, regardless of the fact that we did not have the consent of the Croatian authorities allowing us to enter there. This was supposed to be a trip without an end, or at any rate without a certain ending. I believe it was a Thursday, early in the morning, people started lining up. Even my own company, Kozara Prevoz, charged people for the transport services; that's to say the people who didn't have their own means of transport. Generally people were allowed to leave in their own vehicles, although a large amount of vehicles had been requisitioned earlier on or simply confiscated by military personnel which meant that quite a few people didn't have their own cars. That is why the municipality organised Kozara Prevoz's buses and lorries, trailer trucks, that were supposed to serve as means of transport. On that day, on the 16th, in the morning, people started lining up in a column. In my assessment, there were 4.000 to 4.500 people in that column. I wasn't at the head of the column, I was somewhere midway, in my father's car, where there was my mother, father and one of my brother's children. Mr. Puric was called out of the column. In the column there were first buses, then lorries, and at the end there were personal vehicles, cars. He led the negotiations with the UNPROFOR, who wouldn't allow us to enter Croatia. This stalemate went on for hours. Sometime after noon, one of the representatives of the Danish battalion told us that we should proceed to Dubica where we would be allowed to enter Croatia. Let me go back to explain this to you. There had been earlier discussions concerning this, when Croatia would not allow the convoy to enter. Two alternatives were proposed. One was to enter near Sunja into Petrinja, and the other, which we had suggested, was to go in the direction of Cazinska Krajina, Otoka, whereas Mr. Pasic suggested that we should go in the direction of Travnik. However, we refused to go to Travnik because the trip would be terribly long, and based on the information available to us, killings were being committed over there and all the other atrocities that happened in this war. This was at Vlasic and in the direction of Travnik. Now, as for the route toward Otaka it was automatically refused by Mr. Pasic. It wasn't accepted as an option at all. And we did not discuss these two routes as possible options for the convoy. The only remaining route was that toward the Republic of Croatia and on to third countries. Sometime around noon, or just after noon, the entire convoy set out towards Bosanska Dubica. I was a broken man by then. I was unable to talk. The entire burden of the negotiations fell on Mr. Emin Puric. President of the municipality of Bosanski Novi, Radomir Pasic, was at the head of the convoy, and he led it. He had Mr. Dragomir Drazic with him. As it was entering Dubica the convoy was stopped, and the chief of that municipality did not allow the convoy to enter Dubica. The convoy was kept for hours on that road. As Mr. Puric later told me, he went with a delegation to the bridge in Dubica to negotiate entry for the convoy without any success. The convoy was turned back and we returned to Bosanska Kostajnica. The first bridge in Kostajnica was crossed by the convoy. However, at the next bridge, the great Una bridge, we couldn't cross because we were not allowed to. It was already late at night, 10.00, 11.00, maybe even midnight. When Mr. Pasic signed Emin that we could go back, we led the convoy back towards Bosanski Novi. It was already past midnight when we arrived, at 1.00 or 2.00 a.m. Many people were by that time unable to go back to their homes because Serbs had occupied them as soon as we left or even before we left. The houses that were still available were populated by the people who had come back, and the situation in town at the time was insufferable. I was completely unable to talk by then, unable to speak. It was Monday, and if we needed to, we could now calculate the date even, when an UNHCR vehicle arrived, bringing approval from the German Red Cross that we were ready to receive us and that the Republic of Croatia was prepared to allow us transit. A new departure of the convoy was scheduled for the 23rd of July. There were no longer any problems for the convoy then, and the international force accompanied us all the way, such as the UNHCR, and people who were short of fuel themselves gave us ten or so litres of fuel each. They gave us packed lunch and anything they could afford to give to help, especially the women, children and the elderly and the infirm. The second convoy was significantly larger, perhaps 9.000 or maybe 9.500 people. Later, when we had gotten out, when I was in Croatia, the media mentioned figures of 10 or 11.000 but I still believe it was closer to 9.000 or 9 and a half thousand. Some people who had still not boarded the convoy when it departed stayed behind, and armed soldiers started going door-to-door, forcing them to leave, and a few buses stayed behind the convoy to receive them. Nada Vorona and Ante Sucic, neighbours of mine, were thus forced out of their homes and forced to join the convoy with a delay, together with a number of other people. I don't know how many. We arrived at Karlovac, at the UNPROFOR check-point, and people were transferred from lorries and buses to UNHCR lorries to be taken to the sports hall and the stadium, I believe, in Karlovac, whereas others who travelled in their own cars were allowed passage. That lasted until late at night. Together with my family I left the sports hall to go to Zagreb to my close friend's, and that's where I spent the rest of the war, in Zagreb. Other people in the sports hall were listed, and then whole trains arrived from Germany to take them to Germany. I don't know how many trains there were and to which cities in Germany they travelled. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, we might have a few additional questions. Could I first ask you, you told us that at the second time you were scheduled to leave, that is on the 23rd of July, there were some 4.000 to 5.000 people and then you told us about a second convoy which was significantly larger. And then you said the following. You said: "Some people who had still not boarded the convoy when it departed stayed behind, and armed soldiers started going door-to-door forcing them to leave and a few buses stayed behind the convoy to receive them." This last portion of your testimony, is that about the first convoy in which you left, or was this this second convoy where those who had not boarded were forced to leave their houses by armed soldiers?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: It was the second convoy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what's the source of your knowledge in this respect?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I quoted those two names, the names of my neighbours, and that's what my neighbour Emin told me. And there were also other people in the sports hall told me the same story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was it ever discussed that with the -- with the authorities, that although there was a wish to leave, that those who wished to stay behind would have to join in such convoys as well?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'll try to make it more clear. From your testimony, I do understand that apart from those who boarded the buses, there were others who had not done that yet, and that soldiers went to their houses and forced them on to the buses, which I understood as that these people did not board the buses from their own free will but were forced to do so. Was that ever discussed as part of a scheme to leave the territory of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: No, that was not discussed. But you say that we boarded voluntarily. I mean, who would voluntarily leave their own home and their own town? I think it's -- the way you put the question, we couldn't have discussed whether some people would stay behind because we didn't know at that time that some people were not willing to go. For instance, Kasum Ruhija sent two sons away with his daughters-in-law and children, whereas he stayed behind at home with his wife because he thought things would get back to normal soon, things would calm down. However, six months later, with papers that his family sent him from Germany or whatever state people went to, people continued to leave Bosanski Novi, and the UNHCR evacuated them for family reunion, or maybe the Red Cross evacuated some of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You commented on that part of my question when I said voluntarily boarding the buses, which I meant to say that whereas the others were forced, as you told us, more or less by gunpoint, at gunpoint to board the buses that at least for these steps they are not forced. But you earlier said that all the paperwork that had to be filled in was to establish that you voluntarily and without duress left. Do I understand from your comments on what "voluntary" meant at that time, that it, in your experience, was not voluntary and was not without duress?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Well, of course, in view of all that had happened to me before, from the arrest, the camp, the killing of my uncle, the torchings, the chaos, how can one say that we left of our own will? I mean, who can conceive of such a statement for me to sign? And I had my original documents in my bag. If you wish to see them, I can show you. In the memorandum, it says, on top, the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, pursuant to the decision of the Crisis Staff, number such and such, hereby allows the departure from the Autonomous District of Krajina on a voluntary basis, and I voluntarily sign away my apartment to return it to Kozara Prevoz company and will leave forthwith, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you the owner of your apartment or did you have the right to use it as your residence?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Before the war, in the former Yugoslavia, generally speaking there were very few owners. Very few people bought apartments. People mainly received them from the companies they worked for, and I received mine, as a valuable staff member, because I studied at the university on a scholarship from Kozara Prevoz and later on I joined that company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did any members of your family own any property in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: We had a family house. My father occupied the ground floor. My brother the upper floor. And in the yard, we had a structure for office space. This was the ownership of the two of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What happened to that property?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: As I said, those who were leaving Bosanski Novi had to sign away their property to Republika Srpska to exchange their property or simply produce a document that the property no longer belongs to them. In that complete chaos that reigned, when people started going to the town hall to get those certificates, it was so overcrowded that the administration could no longer cope. Some people got certificates; others didn't. And both times when the convoys were travelling, those documents, those particular documents, were not checked. As far as my father and brother's property, they swapped with some Serbs who lived in Zagreb and drew up a contract on the exchange of real estate. However, when they arrived, when we arrived to Zagreb, this property that we got in exchange turned out to be non-existent. We were cheated. We found the parents of that young man with whom we had signed a contract in Bosanski Novi and who had given us false contract information; in other words, who misrepresented this ownership. So we just signed away our house and he moved in. Later, after the war, we recuperated -- we recovered our property. I got my apartment back and my parents got their house back. My parents now live in Bosanski Novi in their house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. During these negotiations, was it ever discussed whether there would be a possibility for those who wished to leave to ever return, once the war would be over or once the situation would have calmed down?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever ask to those, for example, the Bosanski Novi municipal authorities, whether in the future there would be a possibility to return?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Talking about Mr. Pasic, during these negotiations, did he show any awareness of the reasons why you wished to leave, or did you tell him during these negotiations what urged you to leave the territory of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Of course he was aware of it. He was the president of that Crisis Staff of Bosanski Novi municipality, and he managed the whole thing. He supervised and controlled the situation in full. Mr. Pasic certainly had the situation under his complete control, and he of course was aware of what was going on in town and what was happening to the people. During those negotiations he said that we had to leave and that we may not remain. And that even if we did remain, because the UNHCR representatives were telling us to stay, that they would bring us humanitarian aid, he said that he was unable to guarantee our safety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said he was under -- he was controlling the situation in full. Do you have reasons to believe that he could have guaranteed your safety if he would have wished to do so?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: The authorities of Bosanski Novi municipality, that is the Serb authorities or that Crisis Staff, could have, of course, if they had wanted to. All this was organised. It was no individual incident. I recounted to you the events as they developed. So if he, as the president of the municipality, makes an announcement to us telling us what we had to produce and how we would be allowed to leave, under what conditions, that means that he organised it all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were these conditions ever discussed during these negotiations, that is to give up or exchange your --

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: No. Whatever conditions he set, we said we agreed, just as long as we are allowed to leave, to run for our lives. Naturally, all these administrative requirements, this certificate, that certificate, all that was of no consequence to me. The conditions were in fact set, as far as I see it, so that we would be required to go back to those same institutions once again in case we were wanted, in case they wanted to interrogate us and were unable to find us, so they had another chance to get us. It comes back to me now, and maybe it would be worth mentioning, at those negotiations we set one condition; namely, that the people from the Japra Valley, including Blagaj, Hozici, Agici villages, Celopek, the whole Japra Valley, all those Muslim villages, although some parts of those villages were Serb, they were expelled from their homes on the 11th of May. Some of that population went further up the river towards Ljubija and Sanica, whereas others were escorted into the compound of the Japra mine mining company that was surrounded by a wire fence. On the 11th of May, all of them, women, children, old people, were put on freight rail-cars and were taken towards Gracanica and Doboj. And according to their accounts, women and children were released to go to the free territory that was under the control of the BH army or whatever it was called then, while men were kept in those rail-cars and they were taken back, I don't know exactly where, but some people who managed to escape to Novi from the Japra Valley told me and Emin about it. So we set as a condition that when we leave town they had to come with us. So when we were released from the stadium, from that camp, the Sloboda stadium in Mlakve, they were brought to the stadium, and they stayed there until the departure of the convoy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, just for proper understanding of your testimony, at a certain point you said we want to leave, although you explained under what circumstances you came to this position. I also do understand that Mr. Pasic did not object you leaving, although he put certain conditions. Now, what was the need or under what circumstances he, as you told us, expressed that even if you would not have wished to leave, that you should have left anyhow? Can you recall when he said that and what made him say so? Because you seemed at that time, although under the circumstances prevailing at that time, that you both were of the opinion that you should leave the territory of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, as for leaving, or perhaps running is a better term, that was not on our mind at all initially. However, when all that happened to us happened, we realised we had to run to save our lives. It didn't matter where, just as long as we got away. But I think it was at the bridge that he said it. However, there were so many rounds of those negotiations, in his office, at the municipality, twice in Emin's house, in Dvor, at the bridge, there were so many occasions when we talked that I cannot pinpoint the exact time when he said that. However, there was no question on our side whether we were going or not, whether we had to run or not. And there was no doubt on their side, because everything had been done so that we would leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you have to pay personally for leaving, any additional amount? Were you charged?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't pay any money to leave. I only had to obtain that documentation. I was not leaving the town on my own. I went with the convoy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Hanoteau has more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One question, sir. You stated the following: [In English] "They told us -- [Interpretation] You stated as follows: [In English] "We insisted that we should be allowed to leave. Mr. Dragomir Pasic also invited -- insisted with the UNHCR representatives that we be allowed to leave. They told us in turn that we would not be allowed entry into the Republic of Croatia or, rather, that we would not be allowed to get past the bridge as we used to say. But since the situation was dreadful, we were resolute in our wish to leave. This took place on the 16th of July. "Since the situation was dreadful, we were resolute in our wish to leave." [Interpretation] I would like you to explain to us in what way the situation was dreadful, as far as you were concerned. Can you please give us some examples?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I gave a few examples in my evidence so far. I don't know how far you were able to understand them. There were armed soldiers very well organised and well equipment [as interpreted]. Now if these soldiers come to my flat and force me to leave my home and go to the camp at gunpoint, what more can I tell you? If my uncle had been taken away, killed and his body abandoned at the roadside to stand -- to be there for several days, and if I'm later on invited to identify a body that had been left to rot for several days, maggots and all, if 50 metres away from my home there was the road obstacle and there were guards not allowing us to move around, if after the 11th of May, for several days, Muslims were unable to buy any bread in the town, if people, friends and neighbours, were being taken away, never to be found again, never to reappear, their bodies never recovered, what more did a person need to induce him or her to simply run for life? Of course, my family was well off and probably we could have tried to pay our way out. Whether this would have succeeded or not, I don't know, but I simply did not dare to single myself out of the crowd. Now, the events that unfolded in such a way that Mr. Puric and I, together with friends and neighbours who subsequently joined these negotiations, became representatives and heads of this negotiating team. Let me give you this example. Sometime between the 11th and 31st of May, at any rate it was in late May, that Muslim intellectuals were being called over the radio to organise a team or a council of intellectuals or something of the sort who were to negotiate the surrender of weapons. At that point, people who had already been engaged in politics, like members of the SDA, had disappeared, never to appear, like neighbour Mr. Resad Berberovic, Dzafer Kapetanovic, Mr. Muslimovic. These persons have never been found. I know that they were engaged in politics, like the president of the SDA, Izet Muhamedovic, whose home was 200 to 300 metres away from mine. He was under a sort of house arrest. He was the only one of them there, though. Over the radio we could hear that Panella's party from Italy had intervened on his behalf and made sure that he be kept under house arrest. At one point, he was transferred to Vojnic, into that part of Croatia, from where he was subsequently transferred to Zagreb. I know that at a later stage I met with him in Zagreb; therefore he survived the ordeal. All my friends and neighbours who had college degrees and were people who were members of the authorities, Azmir Celemovic [phoen] who was the police commander in Bosanski Novi, Asim Berberovic, who was judge, Dzemo Sefer, who was the manager of Privredna Banka, Hamdija Ekic, who was the municipality mayor before those elections, we didn't want to set up any sort of council for negotiations because there had been no organisation and there had been no weapons. It made no point to engage in any negotiations because as soon as a person's name was read out over the radio, that person went missing. Later on it turned out that the person had been killed or continues to be missing to this day. For instance, there was one story in front of my house --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry for interrupting. How many friends or members of your family did you lose during the conflict? By "lose" I mean how many people were killed, how many disappeared, how many went missing?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Out of my close family, my uncle was killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about your friends, your acquaintances?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, many of them. I mentioned Muharem Mujkic who was my friend's father. This happened on the 11th of May at Prekosanje. Bosanski Novi is a small town with only 9.000 inhabitants. That was the town proper. Where as the municipality had some 40.000 people, Muslims, Croats and Serbs. We all knew each other or had either business relations or were relatives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me ask you the following question: Before all these events, was there a barracks in Bosanski Novi? Were there regular army units stationed in Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I will have to give you a more detailed explanation. Bosanski Novi was strategically important because of the lay of the ground, of the position of the rivers and bridges. As the army withdrew from Slovenia and Croatia, it did so across the Una and Sana bridges. In that period in 1991, bridges were guarded by the army. All transport went through that route. There was the Montenegrin Battalion, I believe, or some formation. It was a large formation that went through Dvor and then on somewhere, I don't know where. In the centre of the town, there was a small barracks, but the logistical supplies for that barracks came from across the river in Croatia; I believe the place was called Javornik. The barracks was situated across from the stadium and the Una River. I know that a person named Kosta was the commander of the barracks, and I believe he held the rank of a captain. I know this because my wife worked as a secretary to Mr. Pasic in the municipality, and this commander, together with his wife Smilja, lived in the building called Karingtonka next to mine. There were check-points in the town at Svodna, which is en route to Prijedor, at Blatna, which is on route to Bosanska Otoka. There were check-points on all the bridges manned by the army that controlled the traffic, buses, lorries, whatever went past the bridges. My lorries, or that's to say the lorries belonging to the company where I worked went over to Croatia in 1990 and goods were supposed to be loaded over there. Muslims were not able to drive these lorries. Serbs did. Goods would be loaded on to these trucks in Croatia, and then as soon as the situation in Bosnia became favourable they would take the lorries to Serbia to Belgrade, Pancevo and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for your municipality, we've heard evidence and we've seen documents showing that apparently paramilitary formations appeared in your municipality, groups that were not part of the regular army forces. What do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that these isolated incidents by persons who were intoxicated and out of control, there were such cases. In 1991, I was working in my company and some staff members went over to the battlefield in Lipik. This went on for quite a while. Such people, as they returned from the front line, spent most of the time down-town, and they would fire shots, probably out of sheer joy for having survived, and they would mistreat people around the town. There were such isolated outbursts. But in this particular period involving the 11th and the 31st, the setting up of check-points, all of that had been organised, and I'm sure documents and other evidence can prove that these were not isolated incidents. It just came to my mind now that on one of these occasions when we discussed these matters, the idea was put forth that the situation might be settled down if at one of these check-points where there were road obstacles, the -- there was one near to my house in the vicinity of the so-called Vartan [phoen] buildings, mixed teams would be put to man these check-points, consisting of Serbs, Muslims and Croats. However, this idea was resolutely rejected, and there was no more mention of it. In connection with this, there was this one person I knew, called Stole Skondric. We were told that he was the commander, and I'm talking about the period around the 11th. I believe he was planted there in order to create this chaos. Whether he was the formal commander or not, I can't say, because I never saw any such documents. I didn't know who the members of the Crisis Staff were, but we talked amongst ourselves about who possibly members of this Crisis Staff could be and who was it who was in control of the situation in the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question: At the time when you were detained at the stadium, how many people were there at the stadium, how many people were locked up at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I know for a fact that the army compiled a list. I really can't give you an exact figure. This is my assessment, that there were about 1.000 people there. But it's a really rough estimate. At that point, it never really crossed my mind that I should look around and see how many people there were. But I think there were around 1.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Canivell has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, please, can you tell me this: Out of the people who left your municipality, how many did return and set out again, there, where they used to live before the events that you just told us about?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: In my part of the town, namely Vidorija, I believe that all the Bosniaks, Muslims, who wanted to have their properties returned managed to do so. There were of course many houses that were damaged or destroyed, and international humanitarian organisations donated funds to reconstruct them. For instance, in my street, only two young people returned, and when I say young, they are in their 30s. The rest were actually our parents, people aged 70, 80, like my parents. I go back home occasionally, every other weekend, to see my parents. As far as the town and the municipality are concerned, I think that a significant number of people managed to have their properties back, whereas some properties were not given back simply because they were destroyed, there was no interest. I know that several of my colleagues did not manage to get their flats back out of some procedural problems. For instance, because they failed to file their application on time and so on. One of my colleagues, who worked for the customs office and was manager there, did not succeed in getting his flat back. A neighbour, a lady neighbour of mine, who lived in my entranceway and worked at Kozara Prevoz with me and was given her apartment at the same time I was, did not manage to get it back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but, sir, I have to insist, rather than those who recovered their property, I'm interested in the number of people who returned, because you mentioned 14 or 15.000 people who left. Now, how many returned and settled for good back in the area? Well, I'm putting questions to you, but you could tell me maybe also whether the municipality today is part of Republika Srpska or is it part of the federation? If this is the case, can you tell me how many people returned out of the 14.000 or 15.000 people who left when you told us?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that 14.000 or 15.000 people left. I said that I believed the convoy numbered 9.000 to 9.500 people. Since there were people leaving individually, I can't give you the numbers. I wasn't involved in politics then. I'm not involved in now. I never worked for any municipal structures. I really don't know how many people returned. I said that a significant portion of the property was given back. I also said that some of the elderly people went back. Others exchanged properties. I myself live in Bihac now. My parents went back, and out of the six members of my close family only one of my brothers lives with his family in Bihac and only my parents returned to Bosanski Novi. The municipality of Bosanski Novi, or, rather, it is called Novi Grad, because during the war the name of the municipality was changed to Novi Grad, is now part of Republika Srpska. As far as the name is concerned, even the new identity cards read "Novi Grad." Even today if you go to Bosanski Novi to obtain a birth certificate, the birth certificate will read that you were born in the municipality of Novi Grad, which is impossible because I was born in the municipality of Bosanski Novi. Now that it's been renamed, I can have my address read that I live in Bosanski Novi but not that I was born in Bosanski Novi. As regard the identity card, the new identity card I was given, it was corrected, and now it reads that I was born in the municipality of Bosanski Novi/Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see that you cannot give me the exact number of people who have returned. But most of the Muslims and Croats who left, did they return to the municipality, or did they not, according to you? What kind of ratio would you estimate? I mean by that the number of people who left, never to return.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: It was really difficult for me to assess that, but I'm sure that the majority did not return. The difficulty in Bosanski Novi now is not safety but to make a living. People went to different parts of the world, Canada, United States, other parts of Europe. Families have found a living there. Their children go to school there, and they probably decided not to change their life-style now. It was mostly the elderly people with very few young people that returned. Based on the information I heard from my neighbours who still live there, I know that some 16 to 17 people work for the municipal services of Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
