utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you very much, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we have a break, I have a few short questions for you. First, you told us that when you had left the Mlakve stadium, that the people from the Blagaj valley, after having been put on trains, that people from the Blagaj valley then from taken to that same stadium. Do you have any knowledge on whether they were free to leave that stadium and return or whether they were kept there without a possibility of leaving? Please tell us, first of all, if you have any knowledge of it. If not, please tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Well, look, in that period, I did not move around. I stayed in hiding. And only exceptionally, when we went to have talks or negotiations, I left my hiding place. If I understood you correctly, if the interpretation was correct, we were not in rail-cars. We walked back to town from the stadium, which was a one- or two-kilometre walk. So everybody walked back, whereas people from the Japra Valley were in rail-cars, and they were brought to the stadium.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was talking exclusively about the Blagaj, Japra Valley people, whether you know whether they were free to leave that stadium once they were brought there. So I'm not talking about your situation but only about the situation of those who were brought to the stadium from the Japra Valley, whether you know. And if you don't know, please tell us whether they were free to leave that stadium or that they were kept there.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but I don't believe they could move, they were free to leave. Our agreement, in fact the condition that we set, was that they be released with us and join us in the convoy. The authorities accepted that and they didn't make a problem out of it. So they were released from the stadium the same day as we were. I mean, they left on the convoy with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Next question: You talked about places where people were detained or interrogated. You mentioned the Mlakve stadium, you mentioned the police station, you mentioned the fire station, you mentioned a hotel. Could you give us the name of that hotel?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: It was Una Hotel. It was a new hotel in Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Do you know of any other facilities where people were detained or interrogated, apart from those I just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I only know from what other people told me that they were taken to Prijedor, Banja Luka and Gradiska for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then last question. You said you brought some documents if we were interested in looking at them. What kind of documents are these?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Of course. I can take them out of my bag and show you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would please do so and tell us what kind of documents these are.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I will read them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before doing so, would you first tell us, before starting reading it, what kind of documents these are? Because there might be documents we have already in our possession. Of course, I'm not certain about it. So could you please tell us what's the date of the document you are going to read, what is the --

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: These are documents that we had to obtain and later produce in order to be allowed to leave Bosanski Novi municipality, and they are mainly dated the 5th of July, 8th of July, 3rd of July, 6th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. These are the documents you talked about that you'd need to leave the territory of the municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you mind to give them, if only temporarily, to the Tribunal so that they can be copied, that the parties could have a look at these documents in order to see whether there is any doubt in their minds as to their authenticity, and then I take it that you would like to keep the originals yourself.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I then suggest that we ask the Registry to have at least some copies made, and perhaps during the break that the parties can have a look at the documents to see whether there is any authenticity problem involved and that we then consider on the basis of the copies whether it's of any use to have them in evidence. Perhaps, Mr. Josse, someone who can read the documents but I'd rather keep the originals as short as possible in the hands of the Registry and return them to the witness as soon as possible but perhaps by reading the copies to see whether it's of any use to have them in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have two sets so I can give one to Mr. Krajisnik, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll ask, then, the registrar -- how many documents are there, Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Seven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps if you give them to Mr. Usher then we'll take care that during the break they are available for inspection, and that they are copied, and we would then, unless there is any specific problem, I would be inclined to return the originals to the witness. Again, unless there is any specific problem with that. We'll -- yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Does the Chamber have any views as to the tape recording the witness has told us he brought with him to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree with you that I only asked about documents and not about a tape recording. I do understand that -- I take it that you'd like to have access to it in one way or the other which might be easiest achieved by having the tape recording copied first of all. We do understand, Mr. Delic, that you have a tape recording of at least some part of the negotiations. Have you brought that with you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you be willing to give it, if only temporarily, to the Tribunal so that a copy could be made and that the parties and the Chamber could consider whether we would like to have it transcribed and to rely on that material as well for our final determinations? Would you mind to give it? I can't promise that you get that back immediately after the break because copying a tape might take a bit more time.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Usher, you're invited to receive -- Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could the Court inquire as to how long the tape is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It seems to be from a distance -- is it that videotape or is it an audiotape, Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: It's a videotape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a video. And how long is it approximately, how many minutes?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: 40, 45 minutes maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you tell us who recorded it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: It was recorded by people from Bosanski Novi, citizens. It was broadcast on television, the TV of Bosnia-Herzegovina or whatever, and that was part of the TV coverage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then if a copy could be made, Mr. Registrar, then -- Mr. Delic, we --

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I think that this photograph and the persons we saw on the photograph, that's taken from that recording. It's not a secret photograph or anything. There are thousands of them made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take advantage of the opportunity to copy this material. I take it that authenticity, I take it that is a copy already from some other material so that I do not expect there to be any problem. Mr. Delic, we'll have another break, and since we had a late start today, we have limited time left. Could the parties give me any indication as to how much time they would need for questions, and I think in our rules, although not formal rules, it's the Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Of course reserving my position not having seen the tape or the documents, setting that aside I would say 15 to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber of course is not seeking further repetitious evidence. We know that of course this witness was mainly invited for the negotiations, although we gave him ample opportunity to get his way to that point. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That is an issue that I'd like to ask the Chamber about, perhaps in the witness's absence immediately after the break. I have some concerns about the evidence that he gave this morning prior to the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And as to how the Defence are expected to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then hear from you after the break. Mr. Delic, we'll have a break of 20 minutes. We will resume at 25 minutes past 1.00. And I'll inquire into how much -- whether there are any possibilities to sit a bit longer since we had a late start, whether that's it from a point of starting and from any other logistical reasons, whether it would be possible or impossible. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, you wanted to address the Chamber in the absence of the witness, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour. I've looked at the procedure the Chamber set down. At 16D, it says the witness is to be cross-examined by the parties first by the Prosecution and then by the Defence within the time limit set by the Chamber, and then it deals with the scope of the cross-examination that is going to be allowed. Clearly the Defence are anxious to know the what the time limits are going to be set in the case of this witness. Our submission is that we should be entitled to 60 per cent of the time that has hitherto been used by the Chamber in examining the witness. Having said that, we appreciate that up until the first break, he was dealing with events in the municipality. If the Chamber -- that evidence having now been adduced, we seek some guidance from the Chamber as to whether they want that area explored further. We had prepared our cross-examination on the basis of the negotiations and the negotiation on the bridge in particular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That will be shorter, although I'm bound to say considerably longer than 15 to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, you may have noticed that this witness, who came unprepared to some extent, that we started questions at the bridge, to say it this way, and when the witness said that he would need to explain what road took him to that bridge, that the Chamber has not objected to that and has given him an opportunity, although it was not the main reason for calling this witness. So if that is sufficient guidance, if the witness would -- perhaps we would have put a few short questions on it but it's also a matter of a witness who comes here, if you say what happened on the bridge and now go away after you've told us whether there is water under the bridge or whether there was -- that's not exactly the way we treat witnesses here. If that is of sufficient guidance, then the Chamber arranged during the break for additional time this afternoon. That would mean that we would have a short break because we can't stay in this courtroom. We would then move to Courtroom I and would have one and a half hours available. That means that it's considerably more time available, we heard from the Prosecution that they would have approximately 15 minutes. Let's call the witness in and see what we can do in 10 to 12 minutes because otherwise, I might have problems with the Chamber, which is sitting this afternoon in this courtroom. I don't know whether the parties had any opportunity to look at these documents which seem to be -- from what we heard from the witness are mainly the personal documents he needed at that time to get permission to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Not really. I took advantage of the break to speak to Mr. Krajisnik and take some general instructions from him, though I'm grateful a set has been supplied to him as well as to the Defence lawyers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, although we had hoped we could have finished this morning, we might need sometime this afternoon as well, and might come as a bit of a surprise but we found another courtroom to continue at a later stage. I hope that's not too inconvenient to you. But now, first questions will be put to you by Mr. Harmon, counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you, Mr. Delic, to try to focus on the core of the questions put to you by Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could first have the usher's assistance in moving the ELMO? Your Honour, I have reduced the number of questions and therefore my estimate considerably from my earlier estimate, so I just have three areas in which to inquire question about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Delic. My name is Mark Harmon. I'm from the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You mentioned in your evidence the incarceration or the detention of Bosnian Muslims in the Mlakve stadium both -- two separate occasions, the occasion when you personally were there and later when people from the Japra Valley had been brought to the stadium and were detained there until approximately the 23rd of July, 1992. Can you tell us, Mr. Delic, if you are aware of whether Mr. Pasic, the mayor of Bosanski Novi, ever visited the stadium, based on your personal knowledge or based on information you received at a later time?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Then the second area I'd like to ask you about related to your testimony that you were discussing in negotiations an idea that was put forward by the negotiators, by the Bosniak negotiators, that mixed teams, Serbs, Muslims and Croats, would man check-points in Bosanski Novi, and your testimony was the idea was resolutely rejected. Can you tell us who put forward the idea and who rejected the idea?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: It was put forward by Mr. Emin Puric. Or, rather, there was a discussion about whether it was possible to calm the situation down as the UNHCR representative insisted so that we should stay in our homes, and we thought maybe that was the way to achieve it. Mr. Puric therefore said, "Let's put together mixed check-points, joint check-points, where a Muslim and a Serb would be constantly on duty." However, it was said that that is out of the question. So the discussion about that was very brief. Mr. Pasic said that it cannot be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he tell you why it could not be done?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Finally I would like to focus on your evidence that relates to July the 23rd, the 9500 persons who left Bosanski Novi in a convoy. Your evidence this morning was that people did in fact -- a limited number of people did, in fact, remain behind. Then armed soldiers went door-to-door forcing them to leave and a few buses stayed behind to receive them. Can you provide any insight to the Trial Chamber as to the circumstances of why those buses remained behind?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Well, I had already gone by then, so I don't know under what circumstances that happened. But from what I heard from other people, when the people who had decided to stay saw the convoy leaving, and actually passing through, instead of being turned back like last time, they realised that they had to leave too, so they boarded the buses too, and the people who stayed behind said that Serbs had already started going into houses, looting, some people started moving into the now-vacant homes with the intention of staying and even if the house was inhabited, they would turn the inhabitants into the street in order to move into their house, and all the troops were armed, mainly with automatic rifles. So in addition to the number of people who -- or, rather, despite the fact that some people joined the convoy at the last minute, some Muslims stayed behind even then and then found their own way out of Bosanski Novi during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your evidence was that armed soldiers went door-to-door forcing them to leave. I understood that evidence, Mr. Delic, to relate to people who remained in Bosanski Novi after the convoy departed. Then Muslims who had remained in Bosanski Novi were forced out of their homes by armed soldiers. Is my understanding of your evidence correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. But that took all that day. You can imagine how many buses the convoy had, if there were 9500 people, buses, lorries, and passenger cars stretched for over -- for several kilometres. The convoy was passing through town slowly. Some people were unable to start their cars for this reason or another. And while all that was going on, there were armed groups in the town, shooting, going from door to door, making merry. I don't know if they went into each house but I told you about one particular family that was thrown out of their home despite the fact that they had decided to stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you able to estimate the number of people who encountered the circumstances you've just described, people who, on the 23rd of July, wished to remain in Bosanski Novi but who were forced from their homes by armed persons? Any -- give us any enlightenment as to the figures?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I think a small number was forced out that way because the majority had already decided to leave and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And after the convoy of the 23rd of July left Bosanski Novi, are you able to estimate how many Bosniaks remained in the city of Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I believe a couple of hundred.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. Delic. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this moment we are waiting for confirmation that we have interpreters for this afternoon. I see that Mr. Registrar is phoning. Our time is -- will be limited, Mr. Josse. We could continue in Courtroom I, once we have had a break here of 15 minutes only, and that would give us one hour in Courtroom I. Let's see how far we come within that hour and see what can be done. And then we'll have to decide whether -- so provisionally, I would say, the time is set for one hour but still to be reviewed also depending on what happens during that hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm in the Chamber's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll -- Mr. Delic, we will have a short break and we would like then to continue for another hour. We are trying to finish today and we'll see whether we can manage to do that. After the break, you'll first be examined by Mr. Josse, who is counsel for the Defence. We stand adjourned and we will resume in approximately 15 minutes in Courtroom I. --- Break taken at 1.52 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, since we moved courtrooms, could you please call the case again?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. I often apologised in public to technicians and interpreters. I never included at that moment security, which would have been proper to do all those times. The Chamber greatly appreciates the flexibility they've shown this afternoon to make it possible for us to continue sitting. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, earlier today in answer to a question from the learned Presiding Judge you said that after you had been released from the football stadium and whilst you were involved in negotiations, you had a hiding place. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: That's right. There was a shed in my yard behind the house, and I spent a couple of days hiding behind the stacked firewood in the shed. I stayed there so that they couldn't find me at home if they came to look.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: "They" being whom, please?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I mean the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And did the army know that you were a negotiator on behalf of your people?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I think -- by the way, I wasn't a negotiator yet at that time. On the Friday, when I left the stadium, the camp, I was not a negotiator.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The answer you gave earlier was as follows, and I quote: "And only exceptionally when we went to have talks or negotiations I left my hiding place." That suggests that you were a negotiator at the time you were hiding, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if counsel could refer to the location in the transcript where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's page 50, line 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would you like me to repeat my question, Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: It's not necessary. I understood the question. So the entire time from before I was taken to the camp, I told you I shuttled between the house and the apartment, sometimes spending the night on the ground floor of the house, sometimes in the apartment, sometimes in the shed, wherever I felt safest. So in that period, when we started the negotiations, I kept on doing the same thing. However, on Friday, the day after I was released from the camp, I slept in the shed and I did the same thing the following days.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: For two nights; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: No, not two nights. Longer than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How many nights?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Let me just tell you one thing. When I left the camp, I didn't return to my own apartment. I told you before that my -- that the wife, children, and the elderly mother of Sead, Heder were staying at my apartment because their house had been burned down. After I left the camp, they called me to say that two armed soldiers had been to visit and to throw me out of the apartment, and he asked me what to do, whether to resist or to leave the apartment. I told them to feel free to leave, that I'm not intending to try and keep the apartment. I already described the locations between which I shuttled in that period. And until the 23rd of July, I would sleep either in the ground floor of the house or the upper floor or in the apartment or -- sorry, not in the apartment, in the shed or in the little area where I kept firewood.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The negotiation that we see depicted in the photograph at the bridge, were you the chief Muslim negotiator on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: There were two of us, Mr. Puric and myself. As I told you, from our first visit to Dvor through the second visit, we were together, the two of us, and we were occasionally joined by other people, such as Professor Nedim Muftic, nicknamed Nedo, professor of physics, who joined us at the bridge, and Mirsad Brkic, a policeman from Urije. They were standing there and they joined the talks. It was not a formal negotiating team. We simply talked to the other side. On the other side of the bridge, on this photograph and on other photographs, you can see people standing by watching us, trying to get the drift of our negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How were you able to negotiate on behalf of your people, if you were -- if you did not move around? To quote, you say: "I did not move around." How were you able to represent people and know what people wanted? Bosniak people, I mean by that.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I have told you already, the town was divided by check-points and road obstacles called hedgehogs. It was impossible to move around town because the check-points were manned by patrols who checked everybody trying to pass through. They looked at everybody's IDs. I left my home to go to the shed and so on. So I moved within the circle of these several surrounding houses, and I would also go to the bridge to negotiate. I also said this morning that when Mr. Puric and I returned from Dvor, that late afternoon, there would be 10 to 20 people in the neighbouring houses, all of them come to see us, to ask what we had talked about, how things were going, where we had been. So I'm telling you again, it's not that we were elected representatives of the Muslim people at the time. We simply found ourselves in a situation where we represented them as negotiators.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In earlier negotiations, someone called Sifet Barjaktarevic had been involved. Why was he no longer involved in July? If you didn't pick up the name because of my awful pronunciation, I will spell it out, B-a-r-j-a-k-t-a-r-e-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I don't know that man. He did not attend the negotiations with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about someone called Fikret Hamedjagic [phoen]? Does that name mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I know the name Fikret, but I don't know the last name. I think -- I think the man is from the Japra Valley. Maybe he appeared on behalf of the group of people from the Japra Valley that I told you about earlier, but he wasn't in town with us for the negotiations. Maybe he represented the people from the Japra Valley. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And is your evidence that the SDA leadership had simply all disappeared or been eliminated and that is why non-political leaders emerged from your community?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't make that connection in quite that way. I would say that all the people that I enumerated, all from the same neighbourhood, Professor Dzafer Kapetanovic, economist, Mr. Resad Berberovic, also economist, Mr. Ibro Muslimovic, and Mr. Izet Muhamedagic, a lawyer, were representatives of the SDA. From what I know, the three had never been found after they went missing. Their bodies were never found. As for Mr. Muhamedagic, I said earlier that he was under house arrest, and there was news on the radio and television that some party called Panella's party interceded on his behalf, and he was transferred to Vojnic and from there to Croatia. As for us, we first made a call to Mr. Drazic, the two of us or rather three of us, Azemir Ceric, Mr. Puric and I called him as a friend, asking for his help and told him what our intentions were. And we didn't represent anyone but our own families. The families from the surrounding houses, around 100 people, even without the extended families. However, when news of that trickled out and spread around, that afternoon more and more people came to see us to ask what's going on, what's going on?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How many meetings were there on the bridge?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I think two.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was Mr. Brkic present at both of them?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I'm certain about one meeting. I'm not sure about the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was Mr. Puric present at both of them?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You remain in contact with Mr. Puric to this day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. He's my next-door neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what about Mr. Brkic? Do you have any contact with him?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I used to see him, and I still see him occasionally, because he lives in Bosanski Novi where I go to visit, but we had not been friends before, nor is there anything now that would bring us together.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And as far as you know, is he in the MUP in Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I think so. I don't know whether he's still in the MUP, but I know that he was, even after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So far as the negotiations were concerned, this is back in 1992, did you and Mr. Brkic always see eye to eye? In other words, did you have any disagreements?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Not that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you say that: "There is nothing now that would bring us together." What do you mean by that, please? I will repeat that question in a moment, Mr. Delic. I'll do so now. The question was: You say there is nothing now that would bring you and Mr. Brkic together. What did you mean when you said that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Well, you asked me -- when I said that, I meant that I used to see him in Bosanski Novi because it's a small town, we would run into each other, we were nodding acquaintances but we were not friends or relatives. That's what I meant. We were not even neighbours. I know that his brother went with me to primary school, whereas he lives at the other end of the town, in Urije.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You mentioned a car journey and the fact that you shared a -- that car journey with a Serb and that by mentioning that Serb's name might cause difficulty to that person. What sort of difficulty do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Well, look, anybody who lived through that war and survived all the things that happened during that war never knows anymore what can happen. I agreed to testify in public because I want it to be known what happened there and because I want the world to know the truth. Now, as for safety in Bosanski Novi, there seems to be no problem. However, there can always be a person, an extremist, who can create problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've been happy to name the Serb who facilitated your negotiations with Mr. Pasic. So what's the difference between him and the person who gave you a lift? Or who was in your car, perhaps I should say.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Well, look, Mr. Drazic is an acquaintance and friend of ours. He had business relations with these other two persons and we socialised. He was also a member of the Bosanski Novi authorities. I don't know what his role was, but I believe he was the chief of the general administration department for a while, then he was president or vice-president of the Executive Committee of the Bosanski Novi municipality. That was why I mentioned his name. I'm not sure what you had in mind when you say you've been happy to name him. I can also name the friend who drove the car, but if I do so, I would wish it to remain within these four walls rather than have him possibly encountering problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: For what it's worth, Mr. Delic, and this is as much for the information of the Chamber, it was not the name that I'm at all interested in, it was simply the fact that you weren't prepared to reveal his name that I wanted to explore with you, and I'm quite happy to move on. The stadium. When you were asked --

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: If I may say this, he was not politically active and his name is not important at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm with you on that, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse moves on, so we are going to our next subject, Mr. Delic. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The Mlakve stadium, you were asked some questions about the stadium by the learned judge, Judge Hanoteau, and he used the expression, "Locked up". Would you categorise your stay in the stadium as being locked up?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Well, the stadium was surrounded by guards and soldiers. In -- the soldiers stood immediately next to the wire fence. In the wider perimeter around the stadium, there were groups of soldiers. I know this for a fact because in -- at night-time I could see their cigarettes that they were smoking, and in daytime one could see them standing around. On the stands, the bleachers, one could see soldiers standing guard. The lawyer who worked in the same company I did wore a uniform and stood guard there. His name was Milos. I exchanged a couple of words with him, and he told me that this was a unit from the village of Vodicevo. They were there that day, of course, but otherwise they rotated. They were relieved by other groups. But they were there to guard us. That's -- hence the locked up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You have described a number of people effectively agreeing to be incarcerated in the stadium because presumably they had no other option, or it was their best option. Did I understand your evidence correctly in that regard?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Look, people were afraid of staying in houses, I said that several times, because during the night, this infamous red van would pull up and a man who was in the house would be taken away. That was why we felt safer when we were together with other people, and that's why I believed I was safer to be there with others rather than stay at home. At least this way there would be people who would know that I had been taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why, then, do you agree to be released? Did you have no option? Did you have to leave the stadium at the point of release?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: What else could I have done?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, what I'm trying to explore with you is this: Some people, some men, came to the stadium voluntarily and agreed to be locked up there because it was the worst -- I beg your pardon, it was the best of a number of bad options.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, if someone takes me to the stadium at gunpoint and then, after a while, tells me that I ought to go home, what am I to say to this person? No, I'm going to stay here? I don't know what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't asking about you. You have described being taken there forcibly and being detained; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Other people went there voluntarily because --

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: That was an insignificant number of people. Those were the people who realised that all or the majority of Muslims had been taken to the stadium and they were afraid to stay at their homes on their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You had had your pistol removed from you at the point that you were detained; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've explained why you had that pistol and it was licensed to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were you aware of any attempt within the Bosniak community to arm, in the event of there being an armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I said that I was not part of the political circles and I was not politically active then, nor am I politically active now. As far as I know, there were no weapons in Bosanski Novi. That period marked by the war psychosis in Bosanski Novi lasted -- or, rather, started with the events in Slovenia, which were followed by the events in Croatia, and then Bosnia itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So the answer --

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: And I said that, on the 11th, they called out dozens of names over the radio of people who had some weapons. They even mentioned the numbers, reference numbers, of the rifles. It was just a part of the overall scenario in search of weapons and extremists.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to just move on and ask you about the school. You were able to visit the school freely; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. The school is some 20 to 30 metres away from my home. When the citizens of Prekosanje and Urije started arriving, at the head of the column there was a blue combat vehicle, and around them there were armed soldiers and police officers wearing blue uniforms and military camouflage uniforms. The people themselves carried several white sheets which signified surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was the school an elementary school?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: No. It was the Djuro Radmanovic school centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to the departure, and in particular, the role on the day of the departure, 23rd of July, that Mr. Pasic played. Is it right that he was at the front of the convoy?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: On the 23rd of July, I don't think he was at the front of the convoy, whilst on the 16th he was at the front of the convoy throughout the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you for correcting me. And what role did he play on the 16th at the front of the convoy?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: He was -- he too was trying to negotiate with representatives of the international community to facilitate the entry of the convoy into the Republic of Croatia and as well as the return of the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: On that day, did you personally attempt to convince representatives of the international community that - I'm trying to put this as neutrally as I can - that the best option for your community at that moment was to depart?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I wasn't there. Mr. Puric was there on his own, with Pasic, who was at the head of the column, and I believe there was Drazic too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So I need to ask you about the negotiation on the bridge. What attitude did the international community's representative, the gentleman we see in the photograph with the beard, take about the departure of your community?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: He was fully opposed to our departure. He was telling us that we were going towards an abyss, that we should not do that, that he was not mandated to take us out of there, that it amounted to ethnic cleansing, that the UNHCR was not in favour of such actions, that he was there to provide us with humanitarian aid. He said that he was going to get in touch with Zagreb in order to ascertain whether the convoy would be granted entry, but that under no circumstances would this be done under the auspices of the international community. He tried to reassure us and the municipality mayor. He kept saying that the situation would improve and that we should remain in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What stance did Mr. Pasic take?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: He wanted us to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did he say why to the international negotiator?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I don't know how exactly he put it, or whether he said anything, but there was no need for him to talk about it. One could clearly see that. I believe that he said during these negotiations that the international community had to make it possible for us to leave and that they should not prevent us from leaving, that we had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did he explain why he was unable to guarantee the safety of your community?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: No. There was no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why was there no need for that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: It's like in mathematics when there are some common knowledge matters that you need not explain, because I have previously explained to you what the situation was like in our town. If I'm in a situation where I have to bury my uncle with ten bullets in his body and he was just an administrator in a kindergarten, nothing more, without me being able to arrange for a prayer at his burial or anything else, then this is quite telling of the situation in the town in general. I believe my earlier testimony showed this quite clearly, although I may have omitted to say many things.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, there is no dispute that the situation for Muslims in your municipality, in your city, in June/July of 1992, was utterly untenable. The question I'm asking you is whether the municipal authorities could do anything to help you, and in particular, whether Mr. Pasic had any control over renegade police and renegade army units. And whilst I'm happy for you to answer that and tell the Chamber your view on that particular subject, I'm specifically asking you whether anyone asked him during the course of the negotiations, "Why can't you as mayor of this municipality, do something to protect these Muslim people?"

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I'm going to object to the question. It is a compound question, and it assumes facts that are not in evidence at this point. I think the question should be broken down into a series of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's more than one question; I concede to that. I'll ask the last one first, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please, split it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why didn't you say to Mr. Pasic during the course of these negotiations on the bridge, "You're the mayor of this municipality. Why don't you do something to guarantee our safety?"

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I have to tell you that Mr. Pasic was in control of the situation. This was part of a state system, a state apparatus. These were no renegade armies or renegade police forces. There was a Crisis Staff in place, and there was a war situation in the town, not in June/July 1992 but ever since 1991 that people were being sent to the front line in Croatia, to Lipik in an organised fashion. They were taken there in Kozara Prevoz's buses, and this is the company I worked for, where I was the technical manager, and although I held that post I wasn't the one organising these buses. Mr. Pasic wanted to protect the Muslims --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Mr. Pasic did not want to protect Muslims.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: -- and Croats, or, rather, if he had wanted to do so, he should have done that much earlier and not on the 11th or the 20th at some negotiations, because these negotiations were all about saving our lives. I told you that it was in one round of these negotiations, I believe it was in Mr. Pasic's office, where we said and suggested that the teams manning these check-points should be mixed, consist of several ethnicities in order to calm the situation down. His answer was no. And there was no further discussion of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And so I go back to the question I just asked. I rather assumed you'd want to say what you have just said before answering the question that I've just asked, which was why didn't you say to the international negotiator, "He's the mayor of the municipality. He should do something to guarantee our safety"?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I think -- or, rather, I don't think -- I know that the international community held separate talks outside our presence with Mr. Pasic and asked that he guarantee our safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Because he says, and this is what I'm putting to you, Mr. Delic, that the situation had spiraled out of his control and he was unable to rein in many elements in both the police and the army, and therefore he couldn't guarantee your safety.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: That's his viewpoint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would like to put a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'd like to get an additional information on one thing. You told us that the municipality wasn't very big and because of that people knew each other. Is that -- that's it, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can even tell you what you're saying is true but back in 1989, Mr. Pasic, as a lawyer, came for a job interview to my company. He was supposed to be hired as a lawyer. We even hired him, but several days later he quit and went over to Krajina Promet, a commercial company, where he worked as a lawyer. So this proves that we all know everything about each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Great. But this -- here is my question: During those violent events, among the military who were in the check-points, who were controlling your street, did you recognise any Serb inhabitants of your municipality who would have transformed themselves into military and into armed forces somehow? Did you recognise any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I told you that people were mobilised in 1991. They were given various assignments, in Lipik and elsewhere, which they had to carry out. I said earlier on that this Stole Skondric, a tradesman, featured as a commander of the town. Mladen Krnjajic, who also worked for this commercial company, wore a uniform, and later on people were saying that he was always together with Mr. Skondric, the commander of the town. And there were many others. Mladen Krnjajic is the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have you ever spoken to Mr. Pasic subsequent to the events that you've described?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: You mean in wartime or after the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: After the war.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. I met him at the Bosna hotel in Banja Luka in May. I was attending a construction industry seminar organised by the Republika Srpska. I represented my company from Bihac, and I saw him at the hotel there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And did you exchange pleasantries with him or ignore him? Or perhaps he ignored you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: It was at night-time, music was playing, and I was passing by his table as he was sitting with a group of people. As he saw me, he stood up, he extended his hand and we shook hands. I asked him how he was doing, he told me that he was working for the Prijedor employment agency. I replied by saying that I was working in Bihac. And that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. A few more questions. As far as you are aware - sorry, I'm going back now to 1992 - did the UNHCR have any private meetings with Muslim families in -- it would be July, just prior to the departure?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I never had such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's a possibility is the best you can say; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you, if I may, a document. This is P11 -- I beg your pardon, D117, MFI. The usher is going to put one on the ELMO, and I've got a hard copy for the witness to look at. This is in both of our languages and seems on the face of it to relate to a departure in October of 1992 of 1560 persons from Bosanski Novi to Karlovac under the auspices of the International Committee of the Red Cross. Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I don't know specifically about that event, but I know that Karlovac, Gradiska and Sisak were some of the destinations that people chose when they were getting away. Sometimes in groups, sometimes individually. But I don't know of this specific event.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can you explain why, on the face of the document, 1560 persons - doesn't say their ethnicity, it's fair to say - were departing in October from Bosanski Novi to Karlovac?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I don't know how you want me to explain why they were leaving. They were leaving because of the war, away from the pressures they were exposed to. I'm not sure that all of them were from Bosanski Novi. Certainly not, because there were not that many people in Bosanski Novi. I mean Muslims and Croats. So it couldn't have been them. However, in later years, as the war continued, things started happening in town itself. Torching of houses, pressures exerted on people to make them leave, and insufferable living conditions. One of my uncles stayed behind with his wife, and his children tried to get him out for a family reunion elsewhere, and I believe it was in 1992 that it finally happened, but the day after they left, their house was torched.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So the position is that a not insignificant number of Muslims remained in the municipality after the 23rd of July departure?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, the witness - I'll read that portion of his answer - said, the question how he could explain on the face of the document, that he said, "I'm not sure that all of them were from Bosanski Novi. Certainly not, because there were not that many people in Bosanski Novi. I mean Muslims and Croats. So it couldn't have been them." That's an answer to the question where you now put to him something totally different. You're asking now whether his position is that a not insignificant number of Muslims remained in the municipality after the 23rd of July. I think you should be more precise then. If it were not 1560 where the witness said clearly that it couldn't be that number where the witness earlier said that a couple hundreds [sic] may have remained, you couldn't put the question in the way you did it. Please reformulate the question or move to another subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll put it a different way, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You're confirming that there were not 1560 Bosniaks in Bosanski Novi on the 24th of July; is that right? There simply weren't that number left?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: I think that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And looking at this document, do either of the two purported signatures, Cedomir Aleksic or Francois Bellon mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DELIC
utterances.text: Never heard those names.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could Your Honour give me a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please take your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Delic. I have nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. Harmon, any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the Bench also has no further questions for you, Mr. Delic, this means that this concludes your testimony. Before I thank you for having come to The Hague, especially at such a short notice, and having answered all the questions, I'd first like to verify whether any of the parties have any problems with authenticity issues in relation to the documents provided by Mr. Delic, so whether there is any objection to returning the originals to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No objection to the authenticity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We maintain a similar position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that means that whatever dispute we might have over these documents could be done on the basis of the copies that were made today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely. I'm being hesitant because Your Honour, with, respect has clearly chosen your words carefully, doesn't amount to an admission into evidence. It's simply no point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying that. But whatever we would like to say, there will be no point where we say we have to look at the originals in order to decide any issue raised --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's certainly our stance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much for that. Then I think we established already that the video which is of course not an original in any way and has been copied by this Tribunal, that we would not need to keep the copy provided to us by Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The Prosecution agrees as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Registrar, would you please be so kind to have the originals returned, both of the documents and of the video? And Mr. Delic, I'd like to thank you not only for coming to The Hague for answering questions of the Bench and of the parties but also for providing us additional documentation, a video that you brought to us. I hope that you'll have a safe trip home again. Mr. Usher, would you please escort Mr. Delic out of the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to thank the parties for staying well within the time limits set. I also would like to thank both interpreters, technicians and security for assisting us this afternoon, which enabled us to allow Mr. Delic to finish his testimony today. We will adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 28th day of June, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24
